Stop hiring humans led to billions of impressions and millions in ARR. But it’s time for the next era.\

Luca Pacioli: Ancient Double-Entry Bookkeeping, published by Mercury. @mercuryfi \
\
A contemporary republication of John B. Geijsbeek’s 1914 English translation of Luca Pacioli’s landmark 1494 treatise on bookkeeping. Redesigned and newly typeset at the exact dimensions of the original 1914 edition, the book brings the translation together with original pages, diagrams and historical material in a new editorial structure.\
\
Pacioli’s text was the first printed description of double-entry bookkeeping, codifying the system of debits, credits, journals and ledgers that became foundational to modern accounting. The subject has particular relevance for Mercury, whose financial tools for businesses are built on many of these same underlying principles.\
\
The section-sewn hardcover features an exposed spine, silver foil typography and a violet-painted top edge, and is housed in a flexographically printed box.\
\

At 21, I was making around £3,000 a month in profit while studying medicine full-time.\

I’d combined three things I was already good at: teaching, building websites and the BMAT medical-school entrance exam.\
\
So I created a course to help other students prepare for it.\

Then one weekend, I couldn’t teach, so I asked if my two friends wanted to run the course without me and get paid for it. Of course they said yes. \

The feedback was just as good as it was when it was just me running it. \

Delegating helped me scale my time, but I also accidentally outsourced the part I enjoyed most.\
\
So, two lessons:\

1️⃣ You don’t need to do everything yourself.\

2️⃣ Be careful not to delegate the work you actually love.\

I used to assume that a successful business should keep growing: more revenue, more people, more complexity.\
\
But there’s a difficult middle ground between a small lifestyle business and a larger performance business.\
\
Once the team grows beyond roughly 12 people, you often need proper management layers and a completely different way of operating.\
\
Every time we’ve reached 15–18 people, things have started to break, and we’ve ended up returning to a smaller core team.\
\
Right now, that’s what I want.\
\
I’ve got a kid, we’ve recently moved to Hong Kong, and I want more space for family, health and life outside work.\
\
Maybe one day I’ll want to build a huge company. But for now, I’m choosing fun, freedom and flexibility.\
\
Because bigger isn’t automatically better. It depends on the life you’re trying to build.

\
When it drains you, everyone feels it.\
\
Including your clients.\

The writing might be the least important part of your book.\
\
I know. Sounds ridiculous.\
\
Most aspiring authors spend months obsessing over the words.\
Editing sentences.\
Polishing paragraphs.\
Trying to sound intelligent.\
\
But beautiful writing doesn’t guarantee a book worth reading.\
\
What matters more is the idea.\
\
Does your book challenge how people see the world?\
Does it give them something worth sharing?\
Does it introduce a framework they’ll remember long after they finish reading?\
\
Think about “The 4-Hour Workweek”.\
The title alone challenges an entire belief system about work.\
\
That’s the power of a perspective-shifting idea.\
\
Your stories, experiences, and writing bring that idea to life.\
But they can’t rescue an idea nobody cares about.\
\
So before you write another chapter, ask yourself:\
\
Is your book built around an idea worth spreading, or are you just filling pages?

Scaling happens with scissors.\

Every entrepreneur wants to add.\

New offer.\
New project.\
New tool.\
New shiny thing.\
\
But every time I’ve cut something mediocre, the business got better.\
\
More profit.\
More energy.\
More focus.\
\
Growth doesn’t always come from doing more.\
\
Sometimes it comes from removing what no longer deserves to be there.

Brands die in the middle.\
\
Most people think good branding means appealing to more people.\
\
So they soften the edges.\
They try to be premium and affordable.\
Bold and safe.\
Exclusive and accessible.\
\
The problem?\
\
When you stand for everything, you stand for nothing.\
\
Strong brands make decisions.\
\
They choose where they sit on the spectrum—and they’re willing to go all the way to a 1 or a 10.\
\
Where is your brand still playing it safe in the middle?\
